nuance.usage_note: Americans say diesel for both the fuel and the vehicle. At a gas station, you might see 'diesel' on the pump next to 'regular' or 'premium'. Note that in Britain, the fuel is also called 'diesel', but gas stations and everyday talk use 'gas' for gasoline, not petrol. You can say 'I drive a diesel' in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Gasoline is lighter and ignites from a spark plug, while diesel is heavier and ignites from the heat of compressed air.
Gas is the everyday American short form for gasoline, not diesel, so a diesel vehicle does not run on 'gas' in the usual sense.

examples.everyday: I'm filling up with diesel because my truck takes it, so I can't use the regular pump.
examples.professional: Our fleet manager wants to switch half the delivery vans from diesel to electric by next year.
examples.analytical: The diesel cycle relies on compression heating the air to ignition temperature, not on a spark, which distinguishes it from the Otto cycle.

nuance.analogy: Diesel is like a thick, slow-burning fuel that catches fire from pressure alone, the way a fire starts when you press a bellows hard.
nuance.etymology: Named after the German engineer Rudolf Diesel (1858–1913), who invented the engine.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable clearly, as 'DEE-zel'; the second syllable is 'zul'.
Saying 'diesel gas'; Americans just say diesel or diesel fuel.

diesel.etymology: From German *Diesel*, who developed a heavy-duty engine in Germany (1892–1897) and perfected it throughout his life.

conversation.text: Make sure you don't put diesel in the rental; it takes regular gas.
Big trucks run on diesel, so truck stops have separate pumps for them.
Diesel usually costs more than regular gas around here.

senses.definition: Synonym of diesel engine.

core.definition: Another name for a diesel engine, the engine that burns diesel fuel by compressing air until it ignites, used in trucks, trains and ships.

pronunciation.tip: Say DEE-zuhl with a long ee and a short final syllable, not dis-ul. The t in motor is a flap that sounds almost like a soft d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a technical descriptor with no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly say diesel engine. In the US, motor usually means an electric machine, so a combustion unit called a motor can sound unusual. You will hear diesel motor in trucking, farm or older mechanical talk, so recognize it but say diesel engine when you speak.

distinctions.note: Same machine; diesel engine is the standard American term, while diesel motor is less common and can sound regional or old-fashioned.
In American usage a motor is usually electric, so a combustion unit is normally called an engine.

examples.everyday: My uncle's old farm truck still has the original diesel motor, and it starts even on cold mornings.
examples.professional: The fleet team asked the vendor whether the replacement diesel motor meets the new emissions standard.
examples.analytical: Thermodynamic models of a diesel motor explain its efficiency through high compression ratios and the timing of fuel injection.

nuance.etymology: Named after Rudolf Diesel, the German engineer who developed the compression-ignition engine in the 1890s.
common_mistakes: Saying dis-el with a short i instead of DEE-zuhl
Calling a gasoline combustion engine a motor, which Americans usually call an engine

senses.definition: Relating to or produced by a flood or deluge.
Pertaining to Noah's Flood.

core.definition: Relating to a flood or deluge, especially in geology, describing deposits left by floodwaters, or relating to Noah's Flood.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LOO. The ending '-ial' is usually pronounced 'ee-ul' in American speech, not 'eye-ul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and somewhat dramatic. It suggests violent or sweeping water, and it is mostly used in technical or literary writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in conversation. You will meet it in geology texts, historical writing about floods, or theological discussions of Noah's Flood. In everyday speech, people say 'flood' or 'flash flood'.

distinctions.note: Fluvial refers to rivers and normal stream action, while diluvial refers to a sudden or violent flood.
Pluvial refers to rain or rainfall, not to floodwater as such.

examples.everyday: After the storm, the creek left a thick diluvial layer of mud across the whole backyard.
examples.professional: The survey team mapped the diluvial deposits along the valley floor before we chose the site for the bridge.
examples.analytical: Early nineteenth-century geologists debated whether diluvial deposits showed a single catastrophic flood or repeated episodes of flooding.

nuance.analogy: Like a bathtub overflowing across the whole floor, leaving a sheet of silt behind.
nuance.etymology: From Latin diluvium 'flood, deluge', from diluere 'to wash away'.
common_mistakes: Confusing diluvial with fluvial (river-related) or pluvial (rain-related).
Stressing the second syllable of the -ial ending instead of the first main syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word for the Flood in Genesis is mabbul, meaning a flood of waters. The RSV uses 'flood' for it in Genesis 6:17, where God announces that he will bring a flood of waters on the earth, and in Genesis 7:6, which gives Noah's age when the flood came. Genesis 9:11 records God's covenant that all flesh will never again be destroyed by the waters of the flood. Second Peter 2:5 refers back to the flood that came on the ungodly world, and the word diluvial describes this Flood tradition in scholarly and theological writing.

senses.definition: Addiction to alcohol.
Specifically periodic alcoholism, characterized by bouts of heavy drinking rather than continuous indulgence in alcohol.
senses.example: His doctor explained that his dipsomania came in bouts, with months of sobriety between binges.

senses.definition: A strong craving for something.

core.definition: An uncontrollable, repeated craving for alcohol, causing periods of heavy drinking; a historical term for alcoholism.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, -MAY-, and the final syllable reduces to 'uh'. The first syllable is short, as in 'dip', and the middle syllable is a reduced schwa.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a serious addiction and can sound judgmental or outdated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use dipsomania today, except in older writing, medical history or literary contexts. Modern American speech and medicine prefer 'alcoholism,' 'alcohol use disorder,' or simply 'alcohol addiction.' If you hear it, it is probably in a historical novel or an old medical text.

distinctions.note: Alcoholism is the modern, standard term in American English, while dipsomania is an old-fashioned word.
Binge drinking describes a pattern of heavy drinking in a short time, while dipsomania describes a long-term compulsion.

examples.everyday: My grandfather used to call heavy drinking dipsomania, but nobody says that anymore.
examples.professional: The clinic now uses the term alcohol use disorder, because dipsomania sounds outdated in patient records.
examples.analytical: Nineteenth-century writers often treated dipsomania as a moral failing, which shaped how families understood addiction.

nuance.analogy: Dipsomania is like a fire that keeps returning, burning hot in cycles rather than steadily.
nuance.etymology: From Greek dipsa, thirst, and mania, madness or frenzy.
common_mistakes: Using dipsomania as a casual word for liking alcohol, when it describes a serious compulsion.
Using it in modern professional or medical settings, where alcoholism or alcohol use disorder is standard.

senses.definition: The removal of ambiguity.
senses.example: The lexical disambiguation relies on looking ahead to identify possible senses.

senses.definition: A page on a wiki containing links to two or more topics with the same name.

core.definition: The process of removing ambiguity so that the intended meaning of a word, phrase, or name is clear.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on AY, in the -ation ending, with a secondary stress on dis. The -guate part sounds like gyoo-ayt, and the final -tion is shun, not tee-un.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It describes a helpful clarification, so it carries no negative judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disambiguation most often in computing, linguistics, and data work, and in everyday talk about Wikipedia disambiguation pages. In ordinary conversation they usually say clarification or making clear what you mean. A natural reply is 'Right, which one do you mean?'

distinctions.note: Clarification is a general, everyday word for making something clearer; disambiguation specifically resolves a choice between multiple possible meanings.
Interpretation is the act of deciding what something means, often broader and more subjective than resolving a specific ambiguity.
Specification defines requirements precisely, while disambiguation chooses one meaning among several already possible.

examples.everyday: Can you give me a bit more context? I need a little disambiguation before I answer that question.
examples.professional: Our entity-linking pipeline performs disambiguation so that Apple is mapped to the company or the fruit based on the surrounding text.
examples.analytical: Disambiguation is never purely lexical; it depends on pragmatic inferences about what the speaker intends in a particular context.

nuance.analogy: Like a street sign that says Main Street with no city name: you need the surrounding clues to know which one is meant.
nuance.etymology: From disambiguate, from dis- (apart) plus ambiguous (having two meanings), from Latin ambiguus.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the middle syllables as dis-am-bih-GYOO-ate; keep the final -ation stress on AY.
Using disambiguation for ordinary explanation in casual speech; say clarification.

senses.definition: Expression in words, either speech or writing.
senses.example: The senator's discourse was full of pauses, but his message about the budget was clear.

senses.definition: A conversation.
senses.example: Over coffee, our discourse drifted from the sermon to the new library branch.

senses.definition: A formal lengthy exposition of some subject, either spoken or written.
senses.example: The preacher gave us a long discourse on duty.

senses.definition: Any rational expression, reason.
senses.example: Nothing in his discourse made sense to me, though he spoke with great confidence.

senses.definition: An institutionalized way of thinking, a social boundary defining what can be said about a specific topic (after Michel Foucault).
senses.example: In Foucault's account, the medical discourse of the nineteenth century defined who could be called mad.

senses.definition: Lengthy, often heated debate over controversial subject matter, particularly within fandom and activist spaces. Sometimes rendered as a proper noun with the definite article (i.e. "the Discourse").
senses.example: The fan forum exploded into a week-long discourse about whether the finale had betrayed the characters.

senses.definition: To engage in discussion or conversation; to converse.
senses.example: After services, the two old friends would discourse for hours about theology on the porch.

senses.definition: To write or speak formally and at length.
senses.example: The pastor discoursed at length on grace, drawing on Augustine and Luther for nearly an hour.

senses.definition: To exercise reason; to employ the mind in judging and inferring; to reason.
senses.example: Given the data, she discoursed carefully, weighing each hypothesis before drawing any conclusion.

core.definition: Spoken or written communication, especially an extended, serious discussion or treatment of a subject.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on DIS, the first syllable of the noun. The verb is stressed on the second syllable, dih-SKAWRS. Pronounce the r clearly in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It suggests a serious, organized exchange of ideas, though it can sound stiff in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use discourse mainly in academic, political, and literary writing, and in news about public debate. In everyday speech, people say conversation, talk, or discussion. You might hear public discourse or political discourse on the news, which sounds natural in that setting.

distinctions.note: Conversation is the everyday word for talking with someone; discourse suggests a more formal or extended exchange, often about ideas.
Dialogue usually refers to a structured exchange between two parties or to a written conversation in fiction; discourse can be a wider public or academic conversation.

examples.everyday: The discourse online has gotten so angry that I avoid reading comments.
examples.professional: Our team wants more civil discourse in design reviews, so people can disagree without personal attacks.
examples.analytical: Foucault argues that discourse shapes what counts as knowledge, not just what people say about it.

nuance.analogy: Discourse is like a river: many voices flow into it, and its direction depends on how those voices meet.
nuance.etymology: From Latin discursus (a running about, argument), from discurrere (to run in different directions).
common_mistakes: Using discourse for a short casual chat, where conversation is more natural.
Stressing the second syllable of the noun, as in dis-KOURS.

discourse.etymology: From Middle English *discours*, borrowed from Middle French *discours* (“conversation, speech”), from Latin *discursus* (“the act of running about”), from Latin *discurrō* (“run about”), from *dis-* (“apart”) + *currō* (“run”).

senses.definition: To deprive someone of a franchise, generally of the right to vote.

core.definition: To take away someone's right to vote or to participate in a group, system, or decision-making process.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -FRAN-, with secondary stress on dis-. The 'ch' is a single sound, like 'ch' in 'chair', and the final -ise is pronounced 'eyez'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes an injustice, usually involving voting rights or access to power.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word often in discussions of voting rights, civil rights, and politics. It is neutral to formal in tone and common in news and civic discussions. For everyday speech, people sometimes say 'shut out' or 'left out' instead.

distinctions.note: Exclude is general and neutral; disenfranchise specifically refers to removing a right, especially the right to vote or to participate fully.
Marginalize means pushing someone to the edge of society or a group; disenfranchise refers specifically to losing formal rights.

examples.everyday: Some people feel disenfranchised by local politics because they never see their concerns addressed.
examples.professional: Our new scheduling tool could disenfranchise part-time staff if they cannot access the shift-swap feature.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that strict identification laws effectively disenfranchise poor and elderly voters without any direct legal prohibition.

nuance.analogy: If a franchise is a membership card that lets you in the door, to disenfranchise someone is to take the card away.
nuance.etymology: From dis- plus enfranchise, from Old French enfranchir (to free), from en- plus franc (free).
common_mistakes: Confusing 'disenfranchise' with 'disfranchise'; both appear in American usage, but 'disenfranchise' is more common.
Using it for any kind of exclusion; it usually implies a loss of formal rights.

senses.definition: American standard spelling of dishonor.
senses.example: He refused to dishonor his grandfather's memory by cheating his partners.

senses.definition: American standard spelling of dishonor.
senses.example: He refused to dishonor his grandfather's memory by cheating his partners.

core.definition: Loss of respect or good reputation, usually because of shameful behavior that brings embarrassment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, AH. The final -or is reduced to a short ur sound; the r is clear in American English.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests shame and loss of honor, and it is used seriously in military, legal, or family contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dishonor for shameful acts that damage a person's or group's reputation, especially in military, family, and public life. In everyday speech they may say disgrace or shame more often. A common phrase is bring dishonor on the family. As a verb, it means to bring shame to someone, and in the US it is spelled dishonor, not dishonour.

distinctions.note: Disgrace is a loss of respect caused by a shameful event and is often used for public scandal; dishonor is more about losing one's honor or integrity.
Shame is a feeling of embarrassment or guilt; dishonor is the loss of respect or reputation that others see.

examples.everyday: Lying to your mom about where you were would bring dishonor on the whole family, so tell her the truth.
examples.professional: The manager's conduct brought dishonor on the company, and the board has asked for a full review.
examples.analytical: For the ancient writer, dishonor was not a private feeling but a public loss of standing in the community.

nuance.analogy: Dishonor is like a stain on a white shirt: it may be small, but everyone notices and it is hard to fully remove.
nuance.etymology: From Old French deshonor, from des- (not) and honor, from Latin honor.
common_mistakes: Using British spelling dishonour in American writing.
Confusing dishonor with dishonest, which describes a person who deceives rather than someone who has lost respect.
nuance.biblical_note: Dishonor in the Bible often translates the Greek word atimia, which means dishonor, shame, or lack of honor. In 1 Corinthians 15:43 the RSV speaks of the body sown in dishonor and raised in glory. John 8:49 records Jesus saying that he honors his Father and the people dishonor him. Romans 1:26 describes dishonorable passions in the context of human sin, showing that dishonor is tied to a broken relationship with God.

senses.definition: The act of disinheriting.
senses.example: His disinheritance by his wealthy father shocked the family and split the estate lawyers' attention.

core.definition: The act of legally excluding someone from inheriting property, usually through a will, a trust, or a court decision.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on HAIR, and the final -ance is reduced to a weak 'unts' or 'ints' sound. Keep the r in the middle of the word, and do not stress the -tance ending.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a painful family or legal outcome, often tied to conflict, betrayal, or a contested will.
nuance.usage_note: In the US this noun appears mostly in estate law, probate court, and family-business discussions. Everyday speakers usually use the verb 'disinherit' or the phrase 'cut out of the will' instead. Lawyers may also refer to a disinheritance clause in a will.

distinctions.note: Inheritance is what passes to heirs; disinheritance is the act of cutting someone off from that property.
Estrangement is an emotional distance between people; disinheritance is a concrete legal or financial consequence, which may or may not accompany estrangement.
Forfeiture is losing a right or property as a penalty, while disinheritance is a deliberate choice by the person who leaves the estate.

examples.everyday: The whole family drama is about a disinheritance nobody has even put in writing yet.
examples.professional: The estate attorney flagged a possible disinheritance issue before we send the trust documents to probate court.
examples.analytical: The novel's central tragedy is the disinheritance of the younger son, which shows how property law can stand in for love.

nuance.analogy: Like being locked out of a house you were told was yours, with the door closed before you knock.
nuance.etymology: From disinherit (verb) + -ance, from Old French enheriter, from Latin heres 'heir'.
common_mistakes: Using disinheritance to mean an inheritance, which is the opposite meaning.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'dis-in-her-IT-ance'; the primary stress is on HAIR.

senses.definition: Out of place; in a place other than is usual.
Disconnected.

core.definition: Moved out of its normal position, especially a bone or joint; also, out of place or disconnected from its usual setting.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, DIS, and the last syllable is a short, reduced 'id' sound, not 'ated'. The middle syllable 'lo' is pronounced like 'low'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. In everyday use it usually describes a physical injury, which sounds serious; in other contexts it describes something out of place.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use dislocated for a shoulder, knee or finger, as in 'I dislocated my shoulder playing volleyball.' It sounds more clinical than 'out of joint' but is what doctors and emergency staff say. Outside medicine, it is used less often and can sound a bit literary for ideas or people who feel out of place.

distinctions.note: A dislocated bone has come out of its joint, while a broken bone has cracked or snapped; both are serious, but they are different injuries.
Displaced is more general and often refers to people forced from their homes or to objects moved from their place; dislocated is more physical or disruptive.

examples.everyday: I dislocated my shoulder when I fell off my bike, so I'm not going to be lifting anything for a while.
examples.professional: The outage dislocated several dashboards, so the analysts had to rebuild their reports from the raw data.
examples.analytical: Heidegger's language of being thrown into the world helps explain why modern people often feel dislocated from their own traditions and history.

nuance.analogy: Like a drawer pulled completely off its track: it still exists, but it is no longer where it belongs.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dis- (apart) plus locus (place), via the verb dislocate.
common_mistakes: Using 'dislocated' for a broken bone; a fracture is a break, while dislocation means the bone has left its joint.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in dis-LOH-kay-tid; the stress falls on DIS.
Using 'dislocated from' without understanding that it is used mainly in a literary sense for feelings or places.

senses.definition: Relating to disquisition; fond of discussion or investigation; inquisitive.

core.definition: Inclined to inquire deeply and discuss at length; probing, investigative, and fond of careful examination of ideas.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, KWIZ. The qu is pronounced 'kw', and the -ive ending is a short 'iv'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it praises curiosity and rigor but can sound slightly pedantic if the person talks too much.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in writing, reviews and literary or academic prose. In speech it sounds formal, so people more often say 'inquisitive', 'curious' or 'probing'. It can describe a person's mind or style of questioning.

distinctions.note: Inquisitive is common and means curious and asking questions. Disquisitive is more formal and suggests extended, systematic investigation or discussion.
Discursive means wandering from topic to topic. Disquisitive suggests a focused, thorough inquiry rather than a rambling one.

examples.everyday: My roommate gets disquisitive after a beer, asking why the universe exists and whether time is real.
examples.professional: Her disquisitive style in code reviews pushed the team to justify every design choice before we shipped.
examples.analytical: Newman's disquisitive treatment of doctrine invites the reader to test each claim against the evidence.

nuance.analogy: A disquisitive mind is like a careful detective who keeps asking one more question until the whole case is clear.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin disquisitivus, from disquisitio, from disquirere 'to search out'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'disquieting', which means unsettling or troubling.
Using it for simple curiosity, when 'curious' or 'inquisitive' would be more natural.

senses.definition: To throw into confusion or disorder.
senses.example: Hecklers disrupted the man's speech.

senses.definition: To interrupt or impede.
senses.example: Work on the tunnel was disrupted by a strike.

senses.definition: To improve a product or service in ways that displace an established one and surprise the market.
senses.example: The internet makes it easier for leaner businesses to disrupt the larger and more unwieldy ones.

core.definition: To throw something into confusion or disorder, or to interrupt its normal course so that it cannot continue as planned.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on RUHPT, and the r is pronounced clearly. The final t is light and released at the end of the word.

nuance.connotation: Negative in everyday use, such as disrupting a meeting or traffic; neutral or positive in business, where 'disruptive' technology is praised.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word for meetings, traffic, sleep, supply chains and technology markets. In tech and business it can be a positive term, as in 'a disruptive startup'. For everyday annoyance, a natural phrase is 'Sorry to disrupt you.'

distinctions.note: Interrupt means stop briefly. Disrupt means stop or throw into disorder something that was running in a regular way.
Disturb usually concerns peace, calm or sleep. Disrupt concerns the normal functioning of a process, schedule or system.

examples.everyday: A loud motorcycle always disrupts my sleep on Saturday mornings.
examples.professional: The new feature could disrupt our release schedule if QA finds more bugs this week.
examples.analytical: Kuhn argues that anomalies do not simply disrupt normal science; they eventually force a shift in paradigm.

nuance.analogy: Disrupting a process is like pulling one thread from a sweater: the pattern unravels faster than you expect.
nuance.etymology: From Latin disrumpere 'to break apart', from dis- 'apart' plus rumpere 'to break'.
common_mistakes: Adding a preposition, as in 'disrupt to the meeting', when the verb takes a direct object.
Mispronouncing it as 'dis-RUP-ter' or confusing it with 'interrupt' in every context.

disrupt.etymology: Latin *disruptus*, from *disrumpo*, commonly *dirumpo* (“to break or burst asunder”), from *dis-*, *di-* (“apart, asunder”) + *rumpo* (“to break”).

senses.definition: Asking if the store will lower its price to match a competitor's.

core.definition: A question asking whether a store will lower its price to match a lower price from a competitor.

pronunciation.tip: 'Price' is stressed lightly and 'match' carries the main stress. The 'tch' sound is one unit, and the 'i' in 'price' is a diphthong that starts with an open vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a customer request that may sound confident.
nuance.usage_note: Shoppers ask this at electronics, home-goods and big-box stores, often showing a competitor's ad on their phone. Staff may say 'We price match Best Buy and Amazon' or 'Only on identical items.' It is an everyday, polite question, not a complaint.

distinctions.note: A price drop is a lower price the store sets; price matching responds to a competitor's lower price.
A coupon is a discount you bring in; price matching is the store adjusting its own price to match another.

examples.everyday: Do you price match? This same blender is cheaper on the website.
examples.professional: Do you price match on bulk orders, or only on retail sales for individual customers?
examples.analytical: A price match policy signals that a retailer competes on trust in its own pricing rather than on being the lowest in every case.

nuance.analogy: Like asking a friend to split the bill because another place down the street charged less: you hope they will meet the fair price.
common_mistakes: Saying 'price-match me' as a command; the usual phrase is 'Do you price match?' or 'Will you match this price?'
Forgetting that 'price match' is a noun phrase too, so 'a price match' is correct.

conversation.text: Do you price match? It's fifteen dollars cheaper online.
Before I buy this TV, do you price match other stores?
Hi, quick question. Do you price match online retailers?

senses.definition: Official designation for currency in some parts of the world, including Canada, the United States, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, Hong Kong, and elsewhere. Its symbol is $.
senses.example: The price of the coffee was four dollars in Toronto.

senses.definition: Money generally.
A unit of reactivity equal to the interval between delayed criticality and prompt criticality.
senses.example: Our reactor physics team reported the insertion as just under one dollar of reactivity.

senses.definition: (historical) Imported from the United States, and paid for in U.S. dollars. (Note: distinguish "dollar wheat", North American farmers' slogan, meaning a market price of one dollar per bushel.)
senses.example: Prairie farmers rallied behind the dollar slogan, demanding a price of one dollar per bushel.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: The basic unit of money in the United States, equal to 100 cents and written with the $ sign.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The first vowel is the 'ah' of 'hot' (the cot-caught merger), and the final syllable is a light, rhotic 'er' with no separate 'ar' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain, factual word for money and prices and carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'a dollar,' 'five dollars,' or 'a buck' (informal). In casual talk, people often say 'bucks,' as in 'It's ten bucks.' When talking about money from other countries, Americans usually add the country name, such as 'Canadian dollars.'

distinctions.note: Buck is informal slang for a dollar and is common in everyday speech. Dollar is neutral and used in writing, formal speech, and prices.
A cent is one hundredth of a dollar. Cents are used for small amounts, as in '50 cents.'
Greenback is informal slang for paper U.S. currency. It is less common today than dollar and is mostly used in news and older writing.

examples.everyday: The coffee is only a dollar more if you want oat milk.
examples.professional: Our revenue came in at forty million dollars, slightly above the forecast.
examples.analytical: The purchasing power of a dollar depends on inflation expectations that are built into every price.

nuance.analogy: A dollar is like a standard ruler for money: it gives every price a common length so people can compare things.
nuance.etymology: From Low German and Dutch daler, short for Joachimsthaler, a silver coin first minted in Joachimsthal (Bohemia) in the 1500s.
common_mistakes: Saying 'five dollar' instead of 'five dollars' when using a number greater than one.
Saying 'dollar' for Canadian or Australian money without naming the country, which can cause confusion.

dollar.etymology: Attested since the mid-16th century, from early Dutch *daler*, *daalder*, from German *Taler*, *Thaler* (“dollar”), earlier *Joachimsthaler*, literally “of Joachimstal”, the town where the original dollars were minted.

senses.definition: Dominionism.
senses.example: Our seminary professor warned that dominion theology misreads Genesis to justify political power.

core.definition: A Christian movement holding that believers should exercise God-given authority over society, government and culture, often by applying biblical principles to public life.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MIN in dominion, and the final syllables are reduced, so it is not DOM-in-ee-on. In theology the stress is on the second syllable, AH, so say thee-AH-luh-jee, not THEE-ol-o-jee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in scholarly description, but often negative in public debate; critics use it to suggest a religious plan for political power, while supporters may reject the label.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly when discussing religion and politics, especially evangelical debates over Christian involvement in government and public schools. Scholars and journalists often use 'Dominionism' or 'dominion theology' as an umbrella label, and adherents sometimes object that the label is a caricature. Saying it casually at a dinner party can sound like an accusation, so use it carefully and name the specific people or movement you mean.

distinctions.note: Reconstructionism is a narrower movement founded by R. J. Rushdoony that argues for applying Old Testament civil law, while dominion theology is the broader idea of Christian cultural authority.
Christian nationalism is a political identity linking religion with national belonging, while dominion theology is a theological justification that may or may not involve nationalism.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's church is into dominion theology, so they talk a lot about Christians taking over local government.
examples.professional: Our policy brief on religious lobbying groups needs a section on dominion theology, since several donors cite it in their letters.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether dominion theology is a coherent movement or a label critics applied to a loose set of Reconstructionist ideas.

nuance.analogy: Like a blueprint for building a whole city from scripture, it treats faith as a plan for public life, not only private devotion.
nuance.etymology: Dominion from Latin dominium, lordship, from dominus, lord; theology from Greek theologia, discourse about God.
common_mistakes: Stressing DOM-in-ee-on, when the stress is on MIN.
Using the term as a neutral name for all Christian political involvement, when it refers to a specific set of views.
Treating it as a synonym for Christian nationalism, which is related but not identical.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew radah (to rule, tread down) and kabash (to subdue) appear in Genesis 1:26-28, where humans are given authority over the creatures. Psalm 8:6 describes humanity given rule over the works of God's hands. Dominion theologians read these passages as a mandate for believers to shape society, while many other interpreters understand them as responsible stewardship under God rather than a license to control others. Matthew 20:25-26 contrasts worldly lordship with the servant leadership Jesus asks of his followers, a passage often raised in response to dominion arguments.

senses.definition: Nonsense; senseless talk.
A servant; a drudge.
senses.example: The lord's drivel hauled water and scrubbed floors before dawn each morning.

senses.definition: A fool; an idiot.
senses.example: Only a drivel would believe that story about the moon landing being staged.

senses.definition: (rare) Saliva, drool.
senses.example: A thin line of drivel ran down the baby's chin while she slept.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To talk nonsense; to talk senselessly; to drool.
senses.example: Stop driveling about conspiracies and help me finish this report.

senses.definition: To be weak or foolish; to dote.
senses.example: Grandpa drivels over his grandchildren, spoiling them with candy at every visit.

senses.definition: To move or travel slowly.
senses.example: The old truck drivels along the dirt road at barely ten miles an hour.

senses.definition: To use up or to be used up.
senses.example: The battery drivels away overnight if you leave the car lights on.

core.definition: Foolish, meaningless talk or writing; nonsense.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'DRIV-uhl' rather than 'dri-VEL'. Keep the r rhotic and do not add a vowel between the v and the l.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It is a rude way to call someone's words stupid or pointless, and it can hurt if said directly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use drivel when they think speech or writing is worthless, often in arguments or about politicians or reviews. Saying 'That's drivel' to a friend is blunt and can sound rude, so use it with people you know well. The softer alternative is 'That doesn't make much sense.'

distinctions.note: Nonsense is a general word for something untrue or silly, while drivel stresses foolish, rambling talk that has no value.
Gibberish is unintelligible speech, while drivel is intelligible but worthless.

examples.everyday: Don't listen to him, he's talking drivel about the game again.
examples.professional: That proposal is drivel; it has no data and no clear recommendation.
examples.analytical: Much of the commentary dismissed the argument as drivel without engaging its premises.

nuance.analogy: Like a faucet of weak water, the words run on and fill space but carry no nourishment.
nuance.etymology: Probably from Middle English 'drivelen', meaning to drool or dribble.
common_mistakes: Using 'drivel' for a thoughtful argument you disagree with; it means worthless talk, so it is an insult.
Using it as a countable noun, as in 'a drivel'; it is usually uncountable.

senses.definition: Appropriate, required, reasonable care or carefulness.
senses.example: Consumers are required to use their credit cards with due diligence, which includes making sure that strangers cannot find or see their PIN.

senses.definition: A process during which a potential party to a contract evaluates the assets and liabilities of one or more other potential parties, to assess whether it should enter into the contract.
senses.example: Before signing the merger agreement, the buyers completed due diligence on the company's debts and contracts.

core.definition: Careful, reasonable research and checking before making an important decision, purchase, or agreement.

pronunciation.tip: Both words have strong stress on their first syllable: 'DOO' and 'DIL'. The final 'ence' in 'diligence' is weak, sounding like 'ints', and the 'g' is pronounced as 'j' before 'e'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It signals responsibility, though in some contexts it can sound like bureaucratic box-checking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'due diligence' in business, law, real estate, and finance, and sometimes in everyday talk about buying a car or house. It is often used in the phrase 'do due diligence,' meaning to check carefully. In casual talk, say 'check it out' or 'look into it' if you want something less formal.

distinctions.note: 'Diligence' alone means steady, careful effort; 'due diligence' is a formal, often legal process of investigation before a deal.
'Research' is broad and can be academic; 'due diligence' is specifically about verifying facts before committing to a transaction.

examples.everyday: Before we buy that used car, let's do some due diligence and get a mechanic to look at it.
examples.professional: Legal is finishing due diligence on the acquisition, so we shouldn't sign until they confirm the liabilities.
examples.analytical: Due diligence requires the buyer to examine the target's liabilities independently, rather than simply accepting the seller's summary of them.

nuance.analogy: Due diligence is like checking the brakes and tires before a long road trip, not after you crash.
nuance.etymology: 'Due' from Latin debitus, 'owed,' and 'diligence' from Latin diligentia, 'carefulness.' The compound phrase developed in legal English.
common_mistakes: Saying 'do the due diligence' with an article, which sounds unnatural; Americans usually say 'do due diligence.'
Mispronouncing 'diligence' as 'DIL-i-GENCE' with a hard 'g'.

senses.definition: A device that reproduces something, such as printed documents or compact discs; a copier.

core.definition: A machine that makes multiple copies of printed documents or of compact discs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, DOO. The middle -pluh- is a weak schwa, and the t in -cate is a soft flap that sounds like a quick d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a functional, technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say copier or copy machine for office equipment. Duplicator is used for specialized machines, such as disc duplicators that burn CDs or DVDs, or older spirit and mimeograph machines. Calling a standard office printer a duplicator would sound unusual.

distinctions.note: A copier is the everyday office word, while a duplicator is more specialized, often for disc copying or older printing methods.
A printer produces new documents from digital files, while a duplicator reproduces copies from an existing original.

examples.everyday: The church office still has an old duplicator in the back room that prints the Sunday bulletin.
examples.professional: Our production team ordered a new disc duplicator so we can burn the training DVDs in-house.
examples.analytical: The duplicator changed how information spread, letting a single original be copied many times without the cost of hand copying.

nuance.analogy: Like a rubber stamp that presses out identical impressions from one master.
nuance.etymology: From duplicate plus the agent suffix -or, from Latin duplicare, to double.
common_mistakes: Calling an ordinary office printer a duplicator.
Putting the stress on the -kay- syllable instead of the first syllable.

senses.definition: (rare) To describe in dysphemisms.
senses.example: Opponents liked to dysphemize the bill, calling every provision a government giveaway.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To describe something with a harsh or offensive word in place of a neutral one, such as calling a tax increase a grab.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'dys' is pronounced like 'dis'. The 'ph' is a plain f sound, and the final -ize is pronounced 'eyez'.

nuance.connotation: Negative: the word describes a deliberately unkind or inflammatory way of speaking, usually about someone else's position or group.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in conversation. It appears in linguistics, rhetoric and writing about politics and media. In everyday speech people say 'put a negative spin on' or 'use loaded language about'. The word is the mirror image of euphemize.

distinctions.note: Disparage means to speak of something as unimportant or to belittle it. Dysphemize specifically means replacing a neutral term with a harsher one.
Euphemize means to soften a harsh idea with a gentler word. Dysphemize does the opposite, making the description more negative.

examples.professional: In the style guide, we ask writers not to dysphemize customers as 'users who complain' when describing feedback.
examples.analytical: Political commentators often dysphemize their rivals' programs, turning a modest reform into a government takeover.

nuance.analogy: Like swapping a label on a jar from 'spices' to 'mystery powder' to make it sound suspicious.
nuance.etymology: From Greek dys- 'bad, ill' plus phēmē 'speech', on the model of euphemize.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'dye' instead of 'dis'.
Confusing it with euphemize, which means the opposite.
Using it in everyday conversation where 'use harsh language' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: A shaking of the ground, caused by volcanic activity or movement around geologic faults.
A sudden and intense upheaval; a severely disruptive event.
Such a quake specifically occurring on the planet Earth, as opposed to other celestial bodies.
senses.example: Moonquakes are weaker, but an earthquake on Earth can level entire cities.

senses.definition: To undergo an earthquake.
senses.example: Our town rarely earthquakes, so the tremor last night surprised everyone.

core.definition: A sudden shaking of the ground caused by movement of tectonic plates or volcanic activity. Figuratively, a sudden, disruptive upheaval.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the th is voiceless. Keep the 'kwayk' sound clear and do not insert an extra vowel between the th and the k.

nuance.connotation: Negative in most uses because it suggests danger, destruction or sudden disruption, though it can also be used for dramatic change in politics or business.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say earthquake for any shaking of the ground and often shorten it to 'quake' in casual talk. In California people might say 'temblor', but that is more of a regional or news term. Figurative uses like 'a political earthquake' are common in news and everyday conversation.

distinctions.note: A tremor is a small or mild shaking of the ground, while an earthquake is a stronger event that can cause damage.
Quake is a short, informal word for earthquake, used more casually in speech and headlines.
An aftershock is a smaller quake that follows the main earthquake, usually in the same area over days or weeks.

examples.everyday: Did you feel that earthquake last night? My whole bed was shaking.
examples.professional: Our data center has earthquake insurance because the site sits close to an active fault line.
examples.analytical: A sudden shift in economic power can be as disruptive as an earthquake, even though the ground stays where it was.

nuance.analogy: An earthquake is like a rug being yanked out from under a house: everything that seemed stable suddenly moves.
nuance.etymology: From earth plus quake, from Old English cwacian, to tremble or shake.
common_mistakes: Saying 'earth quake' as two words; the standard spelling is one word.
Mispronouncing the first syllable as 'ear'; it is 'URTH', with the stressed r sound from 'bird'.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture earthquakes often appear as signs of God's power or judgment. The Hebrew word ra'ash (רַעַשׁ) refers to a shaking or tumult, and the Greek word seismos (σεισμός) means a shaking or earthquake. 1 Kings 19:11 (RSV) describes Elijah on the mountain, where the Lord was not in the earthquake, showing God is not identified with a natural force. Matthew 27:54 (RSV) reports that the centurion and those with him saw the earthquake at Jesus' death and were filled with awe. Revelation 6:12 (RSV) describes a great earthquake in the apocalyptic vision of the sixth seal.

senses.definition: In an eccentric manner.

core.definition: In an unusual, odd or unconventional way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SEN, and the final -ly is a clear 'lee' sound. Do not reduce the last syllable to 'lih'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative; it describes how someone acts, dresses or designs something in an unusual way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eccentrically mostly in writing or descriptions, such as eccentrically dressed or eccentrically decorated. In casual speech people more often say in an odd way or in a weird way.

distinctions.note: Oddly is plain and common; eccentrically is more descriptive and somewhat more formal.
Unconventionally emphasizes breaking rules or customs; eccentrically emphasizes an odd personal style.

examples.everyday: He dressed eccentrically for the party, with a top hat and bright green sneakers.
examples.professional: The design team organized the onboarding flow eccentrically, so new users couldn't find the settings page.
examples.analytical: Thoreau lived eccentrically by the standards of his town, yet his choices followed a strict moral logic.

nuance.analogy: Living eccentrically is like playing a song in a key nobody else uses: it stands out, though it still has its own harmony.
nuance.etymology: From eccentric, from Greek ekkentros, out of the center.
common_mistakes: Using eccentrically when you mean the person is eccentric; say an eccentric person
Stressing the final syllable instead of SEN

senses.definition: An act or instance of something being edited.

core.definition: The process of revising or preparing text, audio, video, or images to correct, shorten, or improve them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 't' between vowels is often a quick flap that sounds like 'd', so it can be heard as 'ED-ih-ding'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a professional process that can improve or alter a work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'editing' to name the job or process, such as 'video editing' or 'copy editing,' and it is common in media, publishing, and tech. It is usually uncountable, so say 'the editing' or 'some editing' rather than 'an editing'. In casual speech, people often talk about 'the editing' of a film or podcast.

distinctions.note: Proofreading is the final check for surface errors, while editing covers the deeper quality of the work.
Copyediting focuses on grammar, style, and consistency, while editing can also include structure and content.
Revision means rewriting or changing content, while editing is often a broader process that may include revision.

examples.everyday: My sister does video editing for weddings, so she is always busy in June and July.
examples.professional: The editing on the quarterly report needs to be finished before we send it to the client on Friday.
examples.analytical: Editing reveals a text's assumptions, since each deletion asserts what the work did not need to say.

nuance.analogy: Editing is like tuning an instrument: you do not write the song, but you make sure every note sits right.
nuance.etymology: From 'edit' (from Latin editus, 'published') with the suffix '-ing', which forms a noun for the process.
common_mistakes: Saying 'an editing' as a countable noun; it is usually uncountable, so say 'some editing' or 'the editing'.
Confusing 'editing' with 'edition', which means a particular version of a published work.

senses.definition: A person who edits or makes changes to documents.
senses.example: The newspaper's editor rewrote the opening paragraph to make the story clearer.

senses.definition: A copy editor.
senses.example: The copy editor caught three spelling errors and a misplaced comma in my article.

senses.definition: A person who edited a specific document.
senses.example: John Johnson wrote this term paper and the editor was Joan Johnson.

senses.definition: A person at a newspaper, publisher or similar institution who edits stories and/or decides which ones to publish.
senses.example: John is the city editor at the Daily Times.

senses.definition: A machine used for editing (cutting and splicing) movie film or audio tape etc.
senses.example: The old film editor clanked as the technician spliced together the reels.

senses.definition: A program for creating and making changes to files, especially text files.
senses.example: This editor won't open JPG files. I need a graphics editor.

senses.definition: Someone who manipulates video footage and assembles it into the correct order etc for broadcast; a picture editor.
senses.example: The picture editor cut the footage into a tight sequence for the evening news broadcast.

core.definition: A person whose job is to prepare written material for publication by checking, correcting, and improving it, or who leads a publication's content.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The final '-or' is a reduced 'er' sound, and the middle t is a flap, so it sounds close to 'ED-ih-der'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a skilled role and carries no negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use editor for people in newspapers, magazines, book publishing, and websites, and also for software that edits text or images. Depending on the job, you may hear 'copy editor' for someone who checks grammar and style, or 'managing editor' for a senior leader. In casual talk, 'editor' is the normal word for the person who runs or shapes a publication's content.

distinctions.note: A proofreader checks final text for typos and formatting errors, while an editor may change structure, argument, and style.
A publisher is the company or person who pays for and sells the work; an editor works on the content.

examples.everyday: My sister is an editor at a publishing house in New York, so she reads manuscripts all day.
examples.professional: Our technical editor will review the model documentation before we publish it internally.
examples.analytical: Every editor who shapes a text also leaves a trace of their own judgment in what the reader finally sees.

nuance.analogy: An editor is like a tailor who fits a suit: the cloth is the writer's, but the final shape depends on careful adjustments.
nuance.etymology: From Latin editor, 'producer, publisher', from edere, 'to give out'.
common_mistakes: Using 'editor' for a writer; an author writes the work, and an editor changes and improves it.
Mispronouncing the final syllable as 'ee-tor' with a full vowel; in American English it is a weak 'er' sound.

editor.etymology: From Medieval Latin *ēditor*, from Late Latin *ēditor*, from *ēditus*, perfect passive participle of *ēdō* (“give out, put forth, publish”).

senses.definition: The act of ejecting.
senses.example: ejection seat

senses.definition: That which is ejected.
senses.example: Volcanic ejection covered the village in ash.

core.definition: The act of forcing someone or something out of a place, device, or vehicle, often suddenly.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on JEK, and the first syllable is a reduced ih, not an ee or a schwa. The t in eject becomes a sh sound, so the ending is shun, not tion.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses, but it can sound dramatic in aviation or sports contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say ejection in sports for a player or coach removed from a game, and in aviation for the emergency seat that throws a pilot clear of a jet. The phrase ejection seat is very common in American English. In ordinary conversation people often say getting thrown out or being removed.

distinctions.note: Expulsion usually refers to an institutional or formal removal, such as from school or a church; ejection is more physical and immediate.
Eviction is the legal removal of a tenant from a home; ejection is a general word for forcing someone out.

examples.everyday: The umpire's ejection of the coach got the whole crowd booing and the kids cheering.
examples.professional: The ejection of the failed nodes from the cluster triggered automatic rebalancing across the remaining servers.
examples.analytical: The author treats the speaker's ejection from the debate as a procedural matter rather than a question of rights.

nuance.analogy: Like a cork forced out of a bottle by pressure: the object is pushed out suddenly by an outside force.
nuance.etymology: From eject plus the suffix -ion, from Latin ejectio, from ejicere (to throw out).
common_mistakes: Confusing ejection with injection, which means putting something in.
Pronouncing the first syllable as ee or with a full vowel, instead of the reduced American ih.

senses.definition: To decompose by means of, or as a result of electrolysis.
senses.example: We electrolyzed the water to separate hydrogen and oxygen for the chemistry lab.

core.definition: To break a compound into its parts by passing an electric current through it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LEK, and the final -yze sounds like 'ize' in 'size'. Keep the first syllable weak and do not say the word with a long e at the start.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use electrolyze in chemistry labs, metallurgy, and industrial processes, and the American spelling ends in -yze. In casual conversation people say 'split' or 'break down' instead. In a lab report or technical discussion, electrolyze is the exact word.

distinctions.note: Split is a general everyday verb, while electrolyze specifically means decomposing a compound with an electric current.
Decompose can happen through heat, light, or biological action, but electrolyze names only the electrical method.

examples.everyday: In chemistry class we electrolyzed salt water and watched the gas bubbles collect near the wires.
examples.professional: We electrolyzed the sample to remove the metal ions before running the assay.
examples.analytical: Electrolyzing the solution decomposes the compound into its constituent ions, which allows the reaction to proceed.

nuance.analogy: Like taking apart a Lego model with a special tool, electrolysis separates a compound back into its basic parts.
nuance.etymology: From electrolysis, with the verb ending -ize.
common_mistakes: Writing electrolyse, which is the British spelling; in American English use electrolyze.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'lice' or with a stressed ending; the -yze ending is a light 'z' sound.

senses.definition: In an eloquent manner; stated well.
senses.example: The senator eloquently defended the bill, earning applause from both parties.

core.definition: In a fluent, persuasive, and moving way that clearly expresses meaning.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on EL, the first syllable. The final '-ly' is a light 'lee,' and the 'nt' cluster is said smoothly before it.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises the manner in which something is said or written.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eloquently to praise how someone expressed something, especially in speeches, letters, or testimonies. It often follows a verb such as 'spoke,' 'argued,' or 'wrote.' In casual speech people might say 'really well put' instead.

distinctions.note: Clearly describes plain, understandable speech; eloquently adds persuasive beauty and force.
Fluently describes smooth, easy speech; eloquently focuses on the power and persuasion of what is said.

examples.everyday: My neighbor described her late husband's garden so eloquently that I almost felt I'd known him.
examples.professional: Our VP eloquently explained the tradeoff between speed and accuracy in the quarterly review.
examples.analytical: Martin Luther King Jr. argued eloquently that the moral law is higher than unjust statutes, drawing on both scripture and natural law.

nuance.analogy: Speaking eloquently is like playing a melody so clearly that the listener hears the tune and feels its emotion.
nuance.etymology: From 'eloquent' plus the adverb ending '-ly'; the root is Latin 'eloqui', 'to speak out'.
common_mistakes: Placing 'eloquently' in the wrong position; it usually comes after the verb or at the end of the clause.
Using it for simple clarity; it implies persuasive power and style.

senses.definition: The act of flowing or proceeding (of something, quality, or feeling) from a source or origin.
senses.example: The sweet emanation of jasmine drifted through the open window on the warm evening breeze.

senses.definition: That which issues, flows, or proceeds from any object as a source; efflux; an effluence.
senses.example: Perfume is an emanation from a flower.

senses.definition: The generation of the Son and the procession of the Holy Spirit, as distinct from the origination of created beings.
senses.example: In his sermon, the pastor explained the emanation of the Son within the Trinity.

senses.definition: (physics, chemistry) The element radon (Rn)
senses.example: Early physicists called radon an emanation, a gas released by decaying radium.

core.definition: Something that flows or issues outward from a source, such as light, heat, a smell, or a quality or influence.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on NAY, the third syllable. Do not stress the first syllable, and keep the middle vowel as a weak 'uh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It often describes something subtle or refined, such as a pleasant scent or a spiritual presence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use emanation mostly in writing, speeches, or careful discussion of abstract things, like a spiritual influence or a faint smell. In everyday speech, people say 'smell,' 'glow,' or 'vibe' instead. In theology and philosophy, it is a precise technical term.

distinctions.note: Emission is a discharge of matter or energy, often measured, while emanation suggests a more subtle flowing out from a source.

examples.everyday: When I walked into the bakery, the warm emanation of fresh bread made me hungry right away.
examples.professional: The product team noticed a steady emanation of heat from the server rack, so they moved the cooling fans.
examples.analytical: In Neoplatonic thought, the emanation of all things from the One is a way of explaining how the many arise from a single source without diminishing it.

nuance.analogy: Like warmth rising from a sunlit road in summer, an emanation is something that flows outward from its origin.
nuance.etymology: From Latin emanatio, from emanare, to flow out, from e- (out) and manare (to flow).
common_mistakes: Using 'emanation' as a verb; the verb is 'emanate,' as in 'the light emanates from the lamp.'
Using the preposition 'of' where 'from' is more natural, as in 'an emanation from the source.'
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word apaugasma in Hebrews 1:3 means a radiance or reflection, and Wisdom 7:25 (in the Apocrypha, included in the RSV) describes wisdom as a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty. In Christian theology, John 15:26 says the Spirit proceeds from the Father, Greek ekporeuetai, and this passage shaped the doctrine of procession. Hebrews 1:3 says the Son reflects God's glory and bears the very stamp of his nature.

traditions.view: The Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, and the Nicene Creed's Western addition of 'and the Son' (filioque) is rejected as an unauthorized change. The Father is the sole source of the divine persons' origin.
The Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son (filioque), which the Church affirms as the faith of the Western Church and as consistent with the Councils of Lyon and Florence.

Lutheran, Reformed, and Anglican churches generally accept the filioque in the Western creed, while many Baptist and Pentecostal writers focus on the Spirit's work and do not stress the Latin-Eastern dispute.

senses.definition: Synonym of end of story.
senses.example: I'm not changing the schedule, so that's the end of discussion.

core.definition: A phrase a speaker uses to declare that a decision is final and no further debate or argument will be accepted.

pronunciation.tip: The strongest stress is on SKUSH, the middle of 'discussion', and the final syllable is a weak 'un'. Many learners say 'dis-cuss-ion' with equal syllables; in American speech the vowel in the middle is reduced.

nuance.connotation: Negative or authoritarian. It closes debate and can sound dismissive or harsh.
nuance.usage_note: Parents, bosses and coaches use this phrase when they want to stop an argument and make a decision stick. Among friends it can sound annoyingly bossy, so it is better to say it with a joking tone or use 'end of story' instead. A natural reply is 'Fine, I hear you' or 'Okay, got it', since arguing further usually makes things worse.

distinctions.note: End of story is more casual and often a little playful, while end of discussion sounds more like a firm order.
Case closed means the matter is settled, usually after evidence, and it is less harsh than end of discussion.
That's final is a flat, more direct refusal, while end of discussion makes clear that further talk is pointless.

collocations: put an end to the discussion

examples.everyday: You're not going to that party at midnight, and that's the end of discussion.
examples.professional: We're shipping the release on Thursday, and that's the end of discussion for this sprint.
examples.analytical: Invoking the end of discussion closes off argument by authority rather than by reasons, which is why philosophers distrust it.

nuance.analogy: Like closing a door on a conversation while the others are still talking.
nuance.etymology: Discussion comes from Latin discussio, 'a shaking apart'; end comes from Old English ende.
common_mistakes: Using it in a polite setting, where it sounds rude or childish.
Dropping 'of' and saying 'the end discussion' or 'end discussion'.
Stressing the first syllable of 'discussion' instead of the middle syllable.

senses.definition: To reduce strength or energy; debilitate.
senses.example: After being laid off three times in a row, she felt too enervated to look for another job.

senses.definition: To weaken morally or mentally.
(uncommon) To partially or completely remove a nerve.
senses.example: The surgeon chose to enervate the damaged branch to relieve the patient's chronic pain.
senses.label: uncommon

senses.definition: Made feeble; weakened.
senses.example: The long fever left him enervate, too weak to lift a coffee cup.

core.definition: To weaken someone physically or mentally, leaving them tired, drained, or without energy.

pronunciation.tip: The middle syllable is a reduced 'er,' and the final syllable rhymes with 'eight.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something that drains strength, spirit, or morale, often in a heavy or oppressive way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use enervate mainly in writing, reviews, or formal speech, such as describing a sweltering summer or a dull lecture that enervated the audience. In casual conversation they usually say 'wear out,' 'drain,' or 'exhaust.' Using it in a text message would sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Exhaust is common and everyday, and can mean completely tire out; enervate is more formal and suggests a gradual loss of strength or spirit.
Fatigue describes a state of tiredness; enervate describes the action that causes weakness.
Debilitate suggests a lasting or serious weakening of health or ability; enervate can describe mental or emotional draining too.

examples.everyday: That long, hot drive to the coast was so enervating that we slept for two hours after we got there.
examples.professional: Constant context switching and endless status meetings slowly enervate the team's focus and morale.
examples.analytical: Stoic writers argued that passions which do not govern reason can enervate the soul, making it dependent on external goods.

nuance.analogy: Enervation is like a leaky tire: the air escapes slowly until the car can barely move.
nuance.etymology: From Latin enervare, 'to remove the sinews,' from e-, 'out,' and nervus, 'sinew, nerve.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, saying 'en-er-VAYT,' which is wrong for American speech.
Confusing enervate with innervate, which means to supply nerves to a body part, a medical term.

enervate.etymology: From Latin *enervatus*, past participle of *enervo* (“to weaken”).

senses.definition: Tangled or twisted together.
Confused or complicated.
Correlated, even though physically separated; not separable.
senses.example: Physicists confirmed that the two photons remained entangled even after being separated by several kilometers.

core.definition: Twisted or knotted together, or caught up in a complicated situation, such as a relationship, legal problem, or conflict.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'tang,' and make the final '-ed' a separate weak syllable, like 'uld.' Keep the 'g' hard, as in 'get.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, suggesting confusion or difficulty
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'entangled' for both physical knots and complicated situations, such as legal disputes or romantic relationships. In casual speech people often say 'tangled up' or 'caught up,' but 'entangled' sounds natural in news and formal writing. In science, the word also describes quantum particles that remain connected.

distinctions.note: Tangled is more physical and everyday, while entangled extends easily to abstract or complicated situations.
Involved is a neutral word for taking part, while entangled suggests being caught in a difficult or confusing position.
Caught is more casual and suggests being stopped or trapped, while entangled stresses being twisted together with something else.

examples.everyday: I do not want to get entangled in their family drama, so I will just stay out of it.
examples.professional: We got entangled in a dispute over the vendor contract, so the project has been on hold for a month.
examples.analytical: Kant warns that reason becomes entangled in contradictions when it tries to answer questions beyond experience.

nuance.analogy: An entangled situation is like fishing line that has wrapped around itself, where every pull makes the knot tighter.
nuance.etymology: From en- (make) plus tangle, from Middle English 'tangel,' of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Using 'entangled with' for situations where 'entangled in' is the more natural choice.
Pronouncing the final '-ed' as silent, when it is a separate weak syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: In 2 Timothy 2:4, the Revised Standard Version says that no soldier on service gets entangled in civilian pursuits, since his aim is to please the one who enlisted him. The Greek word 'enplekomai' describes being tangled up or involved in affairs that hinder one's real duty.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to enthymeme.

core.definition: Relating to an enthymeme, an argument in which one premise or the conclusion is left unstated.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MAD, the third syllable. The th is voiceless, and the -atic ending is -ik, with a short a in the middle syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term describing a type of argument and carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use enthymematic almost only in logic, rhetoric, and philosophy classes, or when analyzing arguments in academic writing. In everyday speech, people would say an argument with a missing step or an unstated assumption. The word is precise, so use it when you want to point out a specific structure in reasoning.

distinctions.note: Syllogistic describes arguments with all premises stated, while enthymematic describes arguments with one premise or conclusion left out.
Deductive describes reasoning that moves from general premises to a certain conclusion, while enthymematic specifically refers to an argument that omits a statement.
Rhetorical describes persuasive language in general, while enthymematic describes a precise logical structure with a missing premise.

examples.everyday: When I told my roommate the store was closed, I skipped the premise that it was Sunday, so my reasoning was enthymematic.
examples.professional: In the review meeting, I pointed out that the model's recommendation was enthymematic because it assumed the data were complete without stating it.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's rhetoric treats the enthymematic argument as the central tool of persuasion, since audiences fill in the missing premise themselves.

nuance.analogy: An enthymematic argument is like a sentence with a missing word that the listener supplies so automatically that they barely notice the gap.
nuance.etymology: From enthymeme, from Greek enthymēma (thought, argument), from enthymeisthai (to keep in mind).
common_mistakes: Confusing enthymematic with enthymeme, the noun for the argument itself, when the adjective should be used before a noun.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in en-thuh-MEH-mik instead of en-thuh-mih-MAD-ik.

senses.definition: The act of entreating or beseeching; a strong petition; pressing solicitation; begging.
senses.example: Despite her entreaty, the landlord refused to delay the rent increase for another month.

core.definition: An earnest request or plea, often made with strong feeling, asking someone to grant something or do something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TREE, the second syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced EE sound. Do not stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly formal, often conveying emotion or desperation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use entreaty in formal writing, news, or literature. In everyday speech, say plea or request. A natural reply to an entreaty is to say you will think about it or to give a clear yes or no.

distinctions.note: Plea is common and can be used in court or everyday talk, while entreaty is more formal and emphasizes earnest feeling.
A request is neutral and polite, while an entreaty is stronger and more emotional.

examples.everyday: She ignored all my entreaties and kept the car for the weekend.
examples.professional: The team's entreaty for more time was denied, so we will proceed with the original schedule.
examples.analytical: The prophet's entreaty reveals a tension between justice and mercy that the text never fully resolves.

nuance.analogy: An entreaty is like an open hand held out, asking for something with feeling.
nuance.etymology: From entreat, from Old French entraiter, to treat with, with the noun suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using entreaty as a verb; the verb is entreat.
Stressing the first syllable as in EN-tree-tee.

senses.definition: Arousing or likely to arouse envy.
senses.example: Her job offer from the research lab was an enviable opportunity for any young scientist.

core.definition: Something that makes other people wish they had it; very desirable or fortunate.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, EN. The last two syllables are weak, so say them quickly as 'uh-bul'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises something others want, though it can be used with a slight hint of envy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say enviable when praising someone's situation, such as 'You have an enviable view.' It is polite and natural in everyday talk. A typical reply is a modest thanks, such as 'We're lucky.'

distinctions.note: Enviable describes the thing that others want, while envious describes the person who feels the wish.
Desirable is more general and can refer to attractiveness or usefulness; enviable specifically suggests others would envy it.

examples.everyday: Your garden is enviable; my tomatoes never grow this well.
examples.professional: The team has an enviable record of delivering projects ahead of schedule.
examples.analytical: Its enviable clarity allows the argument to persuade even readers who disagree with its premises.

nuance.analogy: Like a window seat with the best view in the stadium: others notice and wish they had it.
nuance.etymology: From envy and -able, 'able to be envied'.
common_mistakes: Using enviable to describe a person who feels envy; use envious for the person.
Stressing the second syllable of the word.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or caused by enzymes.

core.definition: Relating to enzymes, or caused by the action of enzymes in a biological or chemical process.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MAT, the third syllable. The 'z' is voiced, the 'y' sounds like 'eye', and the final '-ic' is short, not 'eek'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise scientific term, and it appears in ads for stain removers and cleaners.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in biology, chemistry, food science, medicine, and in product labels such as 'enzymatic cleaner'. Most people outside science hear it on laundry or drain products. Americans prefer 'enzymatic' to 'enzymic', which is less common and more typical of British writing.

distinctions.note: Enzymic is an older, less common variant, and enzymatic is the standard form in American scientific writing.
Biochemical is broader and covers any chemistry in living things, while enzymatic is narrower and refers specifically to enzyme action.

examples.everyday: That stain remover is enzymatic, so it works well on grass and food stains without harsh bleach.
examples.professional: We saw enzymatic activity drop sharply when the sample sat at room temperature, so we moved the assay to a cold room.
examples.analytical: A purely mechanical account of the cell ignores the enzymatic catalysis that makes metabolism possible at all.

nuance.analogy: Like a skilled assistant who speeds up each step of a recipe without being used up.
nuance.etymology: From enzyme, from Greek enzymos ('leavened'), a term coined in 1877.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, EN-zy-matic, instead of the stress on MAT.
Mixing up the noun 'enzyme' with the adjective 'enzymatic' in formal writing.

core.definition: The younger son of Joseph, ancestor of a major tribe of Israel, and a name for the northern kingdom.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on EE. The 'ph' is an 'f' sound, and the last syllable is a reduced 'um'. Keep the middle syllable quick: 'fruhm'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a biblical name used respectfully in Bible study.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use the name for the person, the tribe, the northern kingdom, or occasionally as a first name. Bible study often pairs it with Manasseh, Joseph's other son. In casual talk, 'Joseph's younger son' is a clear explanation.

distinctions.note: Ephesus is a Greek city in Asia Minor; Ephraim is a person and tribe in Israel, so the similar spelling is misleading.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group spent Thursday talking about Jacob blessing Ephraim and Manasseh.
examples.professional: The curriculum includes the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh in the Joseph unit.
examples.analytical: The prophets often use Ephraim to name the northern kingdom, so the name carries both tribal history and judgment.

nuance.analogy: Like a family name that came to name a whole region, Ephraim names both a son and the people who descended from him.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew 'Ephrayim, probably from a root meaning fruitful.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable; say EE-fruhm.
Confusing Ephraim, the tribe, with Ephesus, the city.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew 'Ephrayim means fruitful. Joseph named his son for God making him fruitful in the land of his affliction, in Genesis 41:52. Genesis 48:13-20 tells how Jacob crossed his hands to bless the younger Ephraim before the elder Manasseh. Hosea 4:17 and Isaiah 7:2 use Ephraim for the northern kingdom, and Hosea 11:8 pictures God's grief over Ephraim.

core.definition: Paul's letter to the church in Rome, the longest of his letters in the New Testament, explaining salvation through faith in Christ.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PIS in 'epistle' and on ROH in 'Romans'. 'To the' is reduced to 'tuh thuh' in fast speech, and the 'Ro' is not pronounced like 'Roe-mahns' or confused with 'Romanians'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the phrase is a standard religious and academic reference with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually shorten it to 'Romans' or 'the book of Romans' in church and Bible study, and cite it as Rom. in footnotes. In a sermon or Bible study you might hear 'Romans says...' followed by a chapter and verse. The full title is mainly used in formal writing or when a listener might not know which book is meant.

distinctions.note: A Gospel narrates the life and teaching of Jesus, while an epistle is a letter addressed to a church or person.
Acts describes the early church's history, while Romans is a systematic theological letter that Paul wrote to a church he had not yet visited.

examples.everyday: Our pastor is starting a series on Romans next month, so we should read the first few chapters together.
examples.professional: For the seminar, I'm summarizing the argument of the Epistle to the Romans in three slides.
examples.analytical: The Epistle to the Romans develops Paul's account of human sin and God's righteousness in a more systematic form than his other letters.

nuance.analogy: Like a carefully reasoned open letter to a whole city, written to explain the core message before the author arrives in person.
nuance.etymology: From Greek epistolē 'letter, message', and Rome, the city to whose church the letter was sent.
common_mistakes: Saying 'Romans' as 'Roe-mans' or confusing it with 'Romanians'.
Dropping 'to the' and calling it 'Epistle of Romans' in formal writing.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word epistolē means 'letter' or 'message', and Paul wrote this letter to the believers in Rome around the middle of the first century.
